current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating experimental antiviral treatments for cats diagnosed with feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), including both the effusive (“wet”) and non-effusive (“dry”) forms of the disease.

FIP is a serious viral disease caused by feline coronavirus (FCoV). Researchers are studying different treatment options to better understand their safety and effectiveness in cats with FIP.

Cats enrolled in the study may receive different experimental antiviral treatments depending on the needs of the patient and study protocol. Cats will be closely monitored throughout the study period to evaluate response to treatment and overall health.
current_roster.tagline: New Hope for FIP
current_roster.name: New Treatments for FIP (Feline Infectious Peritonitis)

current_roster.description: This study is for dogs that have bladder cancer called transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). The goal is to find out if using radiation therapy together with a pill called lapatinib is safe and well‑tolerated by dogs. Researchers will watch closely for side effects and see how dogs respond to the treatment over about 4 months.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study canine bladder translational cell carcinoma.
current_roster.name: Combination of Lapatinib and Fractionated Radiation Therapy for Dogs with Transitional Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description:
This study looks at how a medicine called rapamycin affects aging and health in dogs. Rapamycin has helped mice live longer and stay healthier as they age. The goal of the TRIAD (Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs) study is to see if rapamycin can help dogs stay healthier as they get older, especially with their heart, movement, and brain function.

Researchers want to learn if rapamycin can:

  1. Improve heart health
  2. Help dogs move more easily
  3. Help dogs think and remember better as they age
  4. Possibly help dogs live longer
current_roster.tagline: Help us study how a medication can improve health and lifespan in aging dogs.
current_roster.name: The Dog Aging Project: Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD)

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new type of cancer treatment called CAR T cell therapy for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs.

CAR T cell therapy uses your dog’s own immune cells to help fight cancer. A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and special immune cells (called T cells) are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. These upgraded cells are then given back to your dog through an IV infusion.

Dogs in this study will also receive medications to prepare the body for treatment and to support the immune system during the study. The goal is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective for dogs with metastatic bone cancer.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for advanced bone cancer in dogs.
current_roster.name: CAR T Cell Immunotherapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs

current_roster.description: Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. A safe and common test to find the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis, which means that SLN mapping in dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. The goal of this study is to evaluate SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors and compare the results to other methods.
current_roster.tagline: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
current_roster.name: Minimally invasive sentinel lymph node mapping for dogs with anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA)

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a non-surgical chemotherapy treatment for dogs with brain tumors, particularly gliomas, which are one of the most common and difficult types to treat.

The goal is to test a chemotherapy drug called verdinexor, which may be more effective at targeting these tumors without the need for brain surgery. This treatment is given orally and aims to slow tumor growth and improve outcomes.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test verdinexor, a new chemotherapy for brain tumors in dogs.
current_roster.name: Non-surgical Chemotherapy Treatment for Canine Brain Tumors

current_roster.description:
Feline Lower Urinary Tract Disease (FLUTD) is a common condition that affects many young cats. It can cause frequent trips to the litter box, straining to urinate, blood in the urine, and pain during urination. In male cats, FLUTD can sometimes lead to a complete urinary blockage, which is a life-threatening emergency.

While diet changes and reducing stress may help lower the risk of future blockages, there is currently no cure for FLUTD, and many cats experience repeat urinary blockages.

This study is evaluating whether low-dose radiation therapy can safely reduce inflammation and help prevent future urinary blockages in male cats with FLUTD. Early results from another veterinary hospital have been encouraging, with most treated cats avoiding future blockages after treatment. Researchers hope this treatment can improve quality of life while reducing the need for repeated hospitalizations.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a new treatment to reduce repeat urinary blockages in male cats with feline lower urinary tract disease.
current_roster.name: Low-Dose Radiation Therapy for Cats with Urinary Blockage (FLUTD)

current_roster.description:
This study looks at the best way to treat immune‑mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) in cats. IMHA is a disease where a cat’s own immune system attacks its red blood cells, causing anemia (low red blood cell counts).

The study compares two treatments:

  1. Prednisolone alone (a steroid)
  2. Atopica (an immune‑suppressing medication)

The goal is to see which treatment works better and is safer for cats with IMHA.
current_roster.tagline: Join our study comparing two treatment options for cats with IMHA.
current_roster.name: Treatment of Immune-Mediated Anemia (IMHA) in Cats
current_roster.study_type: Clinical Trial for Immune-Mediated Anemia in Cats

current_roster.description: This study looks at whether a chemotherapy drug called carboplatin can help reduce pain in dogs that have osteosarcoma (bone cancer) in a leg. The researchers want to see if this medication improves how well dogs walk, how active they are during the day, and how well they sleep after treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study how carboplatin can help manage pain in dogs with bone cancer.
current_roster.name: Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to test a new immunotherapy treatment that is injected directly into the tumor. Researchers want to find out how well the treatment works and how safe it is in cats.
current_roster.tagline: Help Investigate a novel immunotherapy for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma
current_roster.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: This pilot study looks at whether a steroid medicine called triamcinolone can help dogs with osteoarthritis feel better. The steroid is given as a shot into a muscle, opposed to directly into the joint. The goal is to see if this reduces limping, lowers joint pain, and evaluate the safety and efficacy of the steroid. This type of treatment has helped people, so veterinarians and researchers want to see if it is also safe and helpful for dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Join our research on using a steroid injection to reduce pain and improve mobility in dogs.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of triamcinolone for osteoarthritis in dogs
current_roster.study_type: Clinical Trial for Dogs with Osteoarthritis
current_roster.top_investigator: Felix Duerr, DVM, MS, DACVS-SA, DECVS, DACVSMR

current_roster.description:
This study is to investigate different treatment protocols in the treatment for copper-associated chronic hepatitis in dogs. Eligible dogs would include dogs that have been diagnosed by liver biopsy with this disease and have not yet started a low copper diet or have received chelation therapy (e.g. D-penicillamine). Exclusion criteria includes if dogs have not been biopsied and diagnosed with this disease and if they are receiving drugs that can affect their immune system.


This is a 6 month long trial where blood work, urine testing, and laparoscopic liver biopsies at 6 months are all covered by the trial. These rechecks are not in addition to the standard rechecks we would normally pursue in any patient affected by this disease.
current_roster.tagline: Help us investigate new treatment options for dogs with copper-associated liver disease.
current_roster.name: Join Our Study on Copper-Associated Chronic Hepatitis in Dogs

current_roster.description: The adrenal glands are small organs in the abdomen that secrete hormones important for normal body function. Adrenal disease is very common in ferrets and affects roughly 25-70% of the North American population. This study’s goal is to establish guidelines for CT scans that could give us better visualization (and therefore information) of adrenal glands. This study will enroll healthy ferrets and ferrets with suspected adrenal disease for full-body CT scans and ultrasounds of their adrenal glands.
current_roster.tagline: Helping improve the diagnosis of adrenal disease in ferrets through advanced imaging techniques
current_roster.name: CT Imaging Study for Ferret Adrenal Disease

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new treatment approach for dogs with immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP), a serious autoimmune disease that causes the immune system to destroy platelets. Very low platelet counts can increase the risk of severe or life-threatening bleeding.

Current treatment for IMTP often includes steroids and other immune-suppressing medications, but these treatments may take several days to improve platelet counts. This study will evaluate a rapid steroid induction protocol using high doses of intravenous methylprednisolone to determine whether it can induce remission more quickly while remaining safe and well tolerated.

Researchers will also evaluate how this treatment affects the immune system using blood samples collected during the study.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a high-dose steroid protocol to help dogs with IMTP achieve remission more quickly.
current_roster.name: Rapid Steroid Treatment for Dogs with Immune-Mediated Thrombocytopenia
current_roster.top_investigator: Charles Talbot, BVSc, MS, MANZCVS (ECC), DACVECC

current_roster.description:
This study is focused on better understanding ductal plate malformations, which are congenital (present at birth) liver conditions that affect the bile ducts in dogs and cats. Examples include von Meyenburg complex, congenital hepatic fibrosis, and Caroli disease.

Right now, very little is known about how these diseases progress over time, and there are no clear guidelines for the best treatment. The goal of this study is to follow pets with this condition and learn more about their long-term health and outcomes.

This is an observational study, meaning your pet’s treatment will be decided by your veterinarian, not the study. Researchers will collect information over time to better understand the disease and improve care in the future.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand long-term outcomes for cats and dogs with ductal plate malformations.
current_roster.name: Clinical Characteristics and Long-Term Outcome in Cats and Dogs Diagnosed with Ductal Plate Malformation

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new type of cancer treatment for dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. The treatment uses your dog’s own immune cells (called T cells) to help fight cancer.

A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and the T cells are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. These upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are then given back to your dog through an IV infusion.

Dogs in this study may also receive oral immunotherapy medications to help improve how well the treatment works.

The goal of this study is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new combination therapy for soft tissue sarcoma in dogs.
current_roster.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T Cells Engineered to Target Soft Tissue Sarcoma with Oral Immunotherapy

current_roster.description:
This study is for dogs that have cancer. Veterinarians and researchers want to see if common vaccines can be repurposed to help a dog’s immune system fight cancer. Dogs in the study will be randomly chosen to receive either vaccines normally used for people (Shingrix or Gardasil) or a rabies vaccine.


At first, dogs will receive 1 to 3 weekly vaccine injections to boost immune response. After that, they will receive weekly injections directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. During the study, doctors will collect small samples from the tumor and nearby lymph nodes at certain times to see how the cancer is responding. Blood samples will also be taken at each visit. The clinical and research team will closely watch how each dog’s tumor changes during treatment.
current_roster.tagline: COTC033: Help us test a new approach to treat cancer by using vaccine immunity in dogs.
current_roster.name: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers in Dogs

current_roster.description:
This study is looking at the connection between feline plasma cell pododermatitis (FPP) and kidney disease in cats. FPP is a condition that causes the paw pads to become swollen, discolored, cracked, and sometimes ulcerated.


Researchers have found that some cats with FPP may also develop a serious type of autoimmune kidney disease called immune complex mediated glomerulonephritis (ICGN). ICGN can cause significant illness and may shorten a cat’s lifespan if not diagnosed and treated early.


The goal of this study is to better understand how often cats with FPP develop kidney disease and how these cats respond to treatment over time. Cats enrolled in the study will be monitored over a 2-year period using bloodwork and urine testing to look for early signs of kidney disease.
current_roster.tagline: A long-term study evaluating the connection between plasma cell pododermatitis and kidney disease in cats
current_roster.name: Studying Kidney Disease in Cats with Paw Pad Disease

current_roster.description:
This study, “Evaluation of autologous protein solution as an anti-inflammatory therapeutic for adult horses with naturally occurring lameness isolated to the medial femorotibial joint,” is sponsored by Zoetis, LLC and supported by the Orthopaedic Research Center and Equine Sports Medicine Service at the CSU Johnson Family Equine Hospital.


The purpose of this study is to compare two different treatments for horses with stifle joint lameness: autologous protein solution [APS (Prostride)] versus a corticosteroid and hyaluronic acid (HA) injection.


Horses enrolled in the study will receive lameness exams, x-rays, ultrasound and treatment of the affected stifle at no cost, plus a financial incentive upon completion of the 24-week study. Owners and veterinarians will not know which treatment the horse receives during the study.
current_roster.tagline: A study evaluating two different treatments (steroids vs an orthobiologic) for horses with stifle joint lameness
current_roster.name: Comparing Treatments for Stifle Lameness in Horses

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate ketamine infusion therapy as a treatment for chronic pain associated with coffin or pastern joint osteoarthritis in horses. Ketamine infusions are used to provide long term pain relief for chronic conditions in humans. While these infusions are frequently used to treat acute or post-surgical pain in horses, their long term effect in horses with chronic pain has not been established.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a novel treatment to provide longer-lasting pain relief for horses with coffin and pastern joint arthritis.
current_roster.name: Ketamine Infusion Therapy for Horses with Chronic Arthritis Pain

current_roster.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.
current_roster.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the ability of a specific stem cell product to alleviate symptoms associated with arthritis in dogs. This stem cell product is a proprietary ‘allogeneic stromal cell treatment’, which means that it contains stem cells collected from a donor dog. The procedure of using cells from a donor dog (“allogeneic” cells) has been utilized in several other research studies (including research performed here at CSU using cells produced at CSU). However, this is the first study at CSU using this specific stem cell product.
current_roster.tagline: Help us evaluate a stem cell therapy for dogs with arthritis.
current_roster.name: Join Our Study Testing a New Stem Cell Treatment for Canine Osteoarthritis
current_roster.top_investigator: Felix Duerr, DVM, MS, DACVS-SA, DECVS, DACVSMR

current_roster.description:
About 3 in 100 dogs are diagnosed with brain tumors each year, and gliomas are among the hardest to treat because they can escape traditional treatments. This study is focused on finding new treatment options for dogs with brain tumors, specifically gliomas, which are one of the most difficult types to treat. Researchers are exploring a new approach called immunotherapy, which helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.


In this study, a small blood sample is taken from your dog to collect immune cells (called T cells). These cells are then modified in the lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. The upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are given back to your dog to target the tumor.


Dogs in this study will also receive a chemotherapy drug called verdinexor, which may help improve the effectiveness of the treatment.


Additionally, dogs can receive radiation therapy, which is currently the gold-standard for treating gliomas in dogs. We hope that by attacking the tumor through immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, we will give dogs the best chance at success.


This is the first study to test this type of therapy in dogs, building on promising results seen in children with brain tumors.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test CAR T cells and verdinexor, a new chemotherapy for gliomas in dogs.
current_roster.name: Immunotherapy (CAR-T) treatment for canine glioma tumors

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new topical anti-inflammatory gel (Tat-PYC-Smad7) for dogs with atopic dermatitis (environmental allergies). Many dogs with environmental allergies need topical treatments in addition to their regular medications to help control skin inflammation and itching.

Tat-PYC-Smad7 has previously been used in dogs and mice to treat inflammatory oral lesions and has shown reduced inflammation and improved healing. This study will evaluate whether the gel can safely reduce skin inflammation associated with atopic dermatitis.

The study is double-blinded, meaning neither owners nor veterinarians will know which skin lesion is receiving the active treatment and which is receiving the placebo gel during the study.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a new anti-inflammatory gel to help reduce skin inflammation in dogs with atopic dermatitis.
current_roster.name: Investigational Topical Gel for Dogs with Environmental Allergies

current_roster.description:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that affects both people and dogs. Dogs diagnosed with AML usually have a poor outlook, and current treatments only extend survival for a short time, typically about 1–2 months.

Researchers are looking for better treatment options for dogs with AML. Many dogs with AML have changes (mutations) in a gene called NRAS, which can cause cancer cells to grow and survive. This study is testing a medication called trametinib, which blocks signals that cancer cells use to grow.

The purpose of this study is to find out whether trametinib is safe for dogs with AML and whether it may help slow down or reduce the cancer. Information learned from this study may also help researchers better understand leukemia in people.

This trial is being led by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory in partnership with the Flint Animal Cancer Center of the Colorado State University Veterinary Health System and is sponsored by the Lutsen Linder Research Fund for Extremely Gorgeous Dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Help investigate new ways to battle acute myeloid leukemia!
current_roster.name: Pilot clinical trial of anti-cancer therapy with trametinib in naturally occurring acute myeloid leukemia

current_roster.description:
Epilepsy is the most common brain disorder in dogs and affects up to 1 in 20 dogs. Many seizure medications can cause unwanted side effects, so there is a need for other treatment options. This study will test a special diet to see if it can help reduce seizures without adding more medication.


This study is looking for dogs that are currently taking at least one anti-seizure medication and still have at least 1 seizure every 2 months. There are two groups in this study:


  1. Group 1 is for dogs that have 2 or more seizures each month. Dogs in this group will first complete a baseline period of up to 3 months, or until they have had 5 separate seizures. After that, they will spend 6 months eating either the test diet or a high-quality maintenance diet.
  2. Group 2 is for dogs that have 1–2 seizures every 2 months. Dogs in this group will first complete a baseline period of up to 6 months, or until they have had 3 separate seizures. After that, they will spend 12 months eating either the test diet or a high-quality maintenance diet. Dogs doing well in the study may be offered an extra 6 months on the study diet.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a special diet to reduce seizures in dogs without extra medication.
current_roster.name: The Effect of a Novel Diet on Epilepsy in Dogs

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new immunotherapy treatment for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) affecting the eye and surrounding tissues in horses, including the eyelids and ocular surface.

SCC is the most common tumor affecting the eye in horses. The goal of this study is to determine if a novel immunotherapy injection can safely reduce tumor size or lead to remission.

Horses enrolled in the study will receive injections of the immunotherapy while standing under sedation. Tumor size and response to treatment will be monitored throughout the study.
current_roster.tagline: Join our study testing a new Immunotherapy for the treatment of eyelid and corneolimbal squamous cell carcinoma in horses
current_roster.name: New Immunotherapy Treatment for Eye Cancer in Horses

current_roster.description:
Diabetes is a common disease in both cats and people. While we know that people with diabetes are more likely to develop tendon injuries that can cause pain and limping, we do not yet know if the same is true for cats.

This study aims to better understand whether cats with diabetes develop changes to the Achilles tendon that may contribute to pain and mobility problems. Researchers will examine tissue samples collected after a cat has passed away to better understand how diabetes affects tendons and other tissues. This information may help veterinarians recognize and treat pain associated with diabetes in future feline patients.
current_roster.tagline: Donate tissue samples to help improve the diagnosis and treatment of diabetic cats.
current_roster.name: Helping Researchers Better Understand Diabetes in Cats

current_roster.description:
This study is focused on improving treatment options for brain tumors in dogs and cats. While progress has been made, many types of brain tumors still have limited treatment options.

The goal of this study is to collect tumor samples to better understand different types of brain cancer. These samples are shared with researchers at CSU and partner institutions around the world. This work may help develop new treatments not only for pets, but also for people with brain cancer.

Your pet’s participation can help advance research and contribute to future breakthroughs in both veterinary and human medicine.
current_roster.tagline: Help us advance brain tumor treatments for pets and humans.
current_roster.name: Biorepository and Advanced Research in Brain Cancer (BARC)

current_roster.description: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.
current_roster.tagline: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
current_roster.name: Near-Infrared Fluorescence Imaging with Indocyanine Green for Intraoperative Detection of Canine Urothelial Carcinoma

current_roster.description: Sarcoids are the most common type of skin tumor found in horses. Right now, there is no treatment that works the same way for every horse. This study is testing a new, experimental treatment to see if it can safely make sarcoids go away (called remission) or at least make them much smaller. All horses in the study will receive the same treatment, which is an injection of an immunotherapy. This treatment is still being studied, so it is not yet known how well it works or how safe it is. The study includes physical exams, blood draws, photos, and injections every 4 weeks for 3 visits, with follow-up appointments at 1 month, 3 months and 6 months post injection series.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for sarcoids, the most common skin tumor in horses.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a New Immunotherapy for Sarcoids in Horses
current_roster.study_type: Clinical Trial for Sarcoids in Horses

current_roster.description:
One of the most lacking areas in veterinary medicine is the ability to diagnose early dementia in dogs and cats. Our team is working diligently on creating simple blood tests that we hope will be able to fulfill this need but first, we need to be able to correlate the blood tests with levels of protein found in the brain.


By collecting samples from dogs and cats who have recently passed away, we’re able to compare these blood protein levels to those of the levels in the brain itself, which should allow us to develop this test in live animals. Our hope is that we will ultimately be able to diagnose early dementia in dogs and cats before symptoms develop, allowing us to better treat the pet to give them more quality time with their family.
current_roster.tagline: Help us develop early dementia diagnostics by contributing samples from your recently deceased pet.
current_roster.name: A Lasting Legacy: Samples Collected from Pets After Death to Study Diseases of Aging

current_roster.description: This study looks at how bones change in dogs with bone cancer in the leg (called osteosarcoma) after radiation treatment. Veterinarians and researchers will test blood and urine to see how much bone is breaking down before and after a special type of radiation treatment called SBRT (stereotactic body radiation therapy). They will compare this information to bone strength, how well the treatment works, and the risk of the bone breaking.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study how radiation and chemotherapy affect bone health in dogs with bone cancer.
current_roster.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new limb-sparing surgery for dogs with bone cancer (osteosarcoma). Instead of removing the limb, this approach uses a custom 3D-printed implant to replace the diseased bone.

The implant is designed specifically for your dog using advanced imaging and is made from a material that can gradually be replaced by your dog’s own bone over time. The goal is to maintain limb function while treating the cancer.

Dogs in this study will undergo surgery followed by chemotherapy and long-term monitoring to evaluate how well the implant works and how the cancer responds to treatment.
current_roster.tagline: A personalized 3D-printed implant designed to replace bone and help your dog keep their leg
current_roster.name: A Limb-Sparing Option for Bone Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description:
A biobank is a secure facility that collects, processes, and stores blood, tissue, and other biological samples for future research.

The CSU Trauma Biobank is collecting samples from dogs and cats with traumatic injuries, as well as healthy pets, to help researchers better understand how the body responds to trauma. By studying these samples, researchers hope to improve the diagnosis and treatment of traumatic injuries in animals while also supporting research that may benefit human medicine.

Samples and health information are stored securely and de-identified before being shared with approved researchers.
current_roster.tagline: Your pet's samples can help researchers develop better diagnostics and treatments for traumatic injuries.
current_roster.name: Building the Future of Veterinary Trauma Care

visible_sc_items.tag_path: centers_Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care, Trauma, and Translational Research
visible_sc_items.label: Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care, Trauma, and Translational Research

current_roster.description:
Staggering disease is a serious illness that affects the nervous system and causes trouble walking, especially in the back legs. It has been seen in cats in Europe for more than 50 years, but it has almost never been found in the United States. In 2023, one case was found in a wild mountain lion in Colorado.

This study is looking for more cases to understand if this disease is affecting cats in the U.S. Researchers and veterinarians are asking for cats that are suspected to have staggering disease to be submitted for testing so they can learn how common it is and what causes it.
current_roster.tagline: Help us investigate the presence of staggering disease in domestic cats across the US.
current_roster.name: Staggering Disease Surveillance Study for Cats

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new immunotherapy treatment for genital squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in male horses. This type of cancer can be aggressive and may require invasive surgery if not treated early.

The goal of this study is to determine if a novel immunotherapy (LTAC) can safely reduce tumor size or lead to remission. Early research has shown promising results, with tumors shrinking after treatment and minimal side effects.

Treatment involves injecting the immunotherapy directly into the tumor to help the horse’s immune system fight the cancer.
current_roster.tagline: Join our research on immunotherapy for genital cancer in male horses.
current_roster.name: Help Us Study a New Treatment for Cancer in Horses

current_roster.description:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is very common in cats and can make them very sick over time. Many cats with CKD have problems like high phosphorus levels in their blood and dehydration. These problems can make cats feel tired, sick to their stomach, or lose their appetite.


Veterinarians often recommend treatments like medicines that lower phosphorus (called intestinal phosphate binders) and fluids given under the skin (subcutaneous fluids). However, there are not many studies showing how well these treatments really work. This six‑month study looks at how phosphate binders and subcutaneous fluids help cats with CKD over time.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for chronic kidney disease in cats
current_roster.name: Investigating the efficacy of intestinal phosphate binders and subcutaneous fluid therapy in the management of feline chronic kidney disease

current_roster.description:
The Brain Health Study is a long-term research program at Colorado State University designed to understand how dogs age and why some develop cognitive decline. Dogs aged 1 year and up are welcome to participate. Depending on your dog's age, size, health, and other factors, our team may recommend one of several research pathways. These pathways may include bloodwork, cognitive testing, owner surveys, and, for some dogs, advanced imaging studies.


Right now, there is no accurate way to diagnose early dementia in dogs, and no single treatment that works well for all cases. The goal of this study is to learn more about brain aging by comparing younger, healthy dogs to older dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand how dogs age and develop cognitive changes.
current_roster.name: Brain Health Study: Helping Dogs Live Longer, Healthier Lives
